Why

Writing is the easy part.

Anyone can make a machine write a blog post now. That's the problem. The internet is drowning in posts nobody asked for, saying things nobody at the company would sign, in a voice nobody has.

The hard part has always been knowing what's true, much more than the writing. What you sell this quarter. What you stopped saying last month. What sales promised a customer on Tuesday. What the founder said on a podcast that contradicts the pricing page.

Your wiki doesn't know. Your brand book was right the day someone wrote it, and nobody has opened it since. Docs rot. Every company is quietly lying to its customers and doesn't know where.

What you get

Everything a content team does, minus the content team.

Approval chains, revisited for Scale

The three chains auditors like, and the one they flag every time.

Approval chains got simpler on Scale: up to 25 approvers, any order, any threshold. This post walks through the three chains auditors like best.

The first is the plain two-step: whoever raised the bill, then a controller. Haldane moved every vendor under €5,000 onto it and cut audit findings on AP by 40%.

The second adds a budget owner above a threshold. Approvers can be added mid-chain without restarting it, so a late sign-off doesn't send the bill back to the start.

Why your close slips in the last 48 hours

The last two days of the close are where the waiting hides. Here is where it goes.

Month-end close takes five days at most teams. Two of them are spent waiting: on a bank feed, on an approval, on the one person who knows how last month's accrual was booked.

The work is done by day three

We looked at forty closes this quarter. In thirty-one, every journal was posted by the third morning.

How the goals work →

Fit

Propaganda is great for some people. It stinks for others.

Great for

  • Founders who sell on calls and say the same brilliant thing 30 times a week, out loud, to one person at a time
  • B2B companies of 5 to 200 people with a lot to say and nobody whose job it is to say it
  • Companies whose website, sales deck and LinkedIn currently disagree about what they sell
  • People who want a blog that ranks without becoming a blog person
  • Teams who are done paying an agency $8k a month for posts that start with "In today's fast-paced world"

Stinks for

  • Content farms. We cap your volume at what you can stand behind. You'll hate us.
  • Anyone who wants 100 SEO pages by Friday
  • LinkedIn growth hackers, thought leaders and people who say "let's double-click on that"
  • Companies with nothing to say. We can't fix that. Nobody can.
  • Novelists. Go write your book. By hand. Like an adult.

Your company already knows what to say. It's just stuck in a Zoom recording.
